title: Java News Roundup: Shenandoah GC, TeamCity CVE, A2A Java SDK, Camel, Gradle, GlassFish, Groovy
gist: A weekly Java ecosystem roundup whose two hardest signals are Oracle delaying the JDK 27 initial release candidate two weeks to align with the August 18 Critical Patch Update, and active in-the-wild exploitation of JetBrains TeamCity CVE-2026-63077, an unauthenticated pre-auth OS command execution flaw. Note a title/body discrepancy: the headline and intro cite a fifth milestone of Groovy 8.0, but the article body actually covers Apache Grails 8.0.0 milestone five.

themes.theme: JDK release-train slippage under CPU pressure

insights.claim: Oracle's Mark Reinhold moved the initial release candidate for JDK 27 from August 6, 2026 to August 20, 2026 so it aligns with the August 18, 2026 Critical Patch Update, citing an increase in the frequency of CPUs.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Security patch cadence is now dictating Java's release calendar — a structural shift that shortens QA windows for every future JDK train.
insights.locator: Mark Reinhold, Chief Architect, Java Platform Group

insights.claim: The RC slip cuts the feedback window on release-candidate builds from five weeks and four days to three weeks and four days, which Reinhold concedes theoretically increases risk.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: A 36% shorter RC soak period is the concrete cost of the alignment — worth watching whether JDK 27 needs an unusual second RC.
insights.quote: This reduces the time available for feedback on RC builds by two weeks, from five weeks and four days to three weeks and four days. That does, at least theoretically, increase risk.
insights.locator: Describing the risks for this change

insights.claim: Reinhold justifies the compressed schedule with historical data: since the six-month cadence began in JDK 10, fewer than half of releases needed a second RC build, and none of the triggering bugs was reported by an end user.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: The stated rationale implies end-user RC testing contributes little to OpenJDK quality — a quiet admission that the community feedback loop on RCs is thin.
insights.quote: since we switched to the six-month cadence in JDK 10 we have needed a second RC build for fewer than half of our releases, and none of the bugs that triggered those builds was reported by an end user
insights.locator: Describing the risks for this change

insights.claim: JDK 27 early-access Build 34 had originally been intended to serve as the initial release candidate build before the schedule change.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: The RC was effectively ready — the delay is calendar alignment, not a quality problem, which lowers the odds of feature cuts.
insights.locator: Build 34 of JDK 27, released this past week

insights.claim: JEP 535, Shenandoah GC: Generational Mode by Default, has been elevated from Proposed to Target to Targeted for JDK 28, making generational the default mode for the collector.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Low-pause GC defaults changing affects latency profiles for every Shenandoah-tuned service — retune before upgrading to JDK 28.
insights.locator: JEP 535, Shenandoah GC: Generational Mode by Default

insights.claim: The non-generational Shenandoah mode will be deprecated with the intent to remove it in a future release, closing off the older configuration entirely.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Teams pinned to non-generational Shenandoah have a finite migration runway — an explicit deprecation clock, not a soft recommendation.
insights.quote: The non-generational mode will be deprecated with the intent to remove it in a future release.
insights.locator: JEP 535, Shenandoah GC: Generational Mode by Default

themes.theme: Actively exploited CI/CD and app-server vulnerabilities

insights.claim: JetBrains TeamCity CVE-2026-63077 lets an attacker with HTTP(S) access to a TeamCity server bypass authentication checks and execute arbitrary operating system commands, and there are reports of active exploitations against unpatched servers.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Pre-auth RCE on a build server is a supply-chain compromise vector, not just a host compromise — treat exposure as a software-integrity incident.
insights.quote: a vulnerability that allows an attacker, with HTTP(S) access to a TeamCity server, to bypass authentication checks and execute arbitrary operating system commands
insights.locator: The TeamCity team has provided additional guidance

insights.claim: Remediation for the TeamCity flaw is upgrading to TeamCity 2025.11.7 or 2026.1.3, with a downloadable security patch plugin available as a fallback for TeamCity 2017.1 and later.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: The patch plugin reaching back to 2017.1 signals JetBrains expects a large long-tail of ancient, unpatchable installs — the exploited population will persist.
insights.locator: Developers are highly encouraged to upgrade

insights.claim: GlassFish 8.0.4 fixes CVE-2026-12605, in which a leaked gfresttoken from the DownloadServlet class allows an attacker already authenticated in the Admin Console to gain full unauthenticated takeover of the GlassFish domain until the token expires.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Token-leak-to-domain-takeover in a legacy app server is exactly the class of flaw that lingers in unmaintained enterprise Java estates.
insights.locator: This release also provides resolutions to CVE-2026-59889

insights.claim: GlassFish 8.0.4 also resolves CVE-2026-59889 and CVE-2026-54515, both related to deserialization with Jackson Databind.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Jackson deserialization remains a recurring CVE source across the Java stack — a persistent audit target regardless of framework.
insights.locator: This release also provides resolutions to CVE-2026-59889

insights.claim: GlassFish 8.0.4 hardens the AutoDeployer and FileArchive classes specifically against files escaping the archive file, addressing path-traversal-style extraction risk during deployment.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Archive-escape protection landing in 2026 shows a decades-old vulnerability class is still being retrofitted into mature Java servers.
insights.locator: The release of GlassFish 8.0.4 delivers bug fixes

themes.theme: Agent protocols moving into mainstream Java tooling

insights.claim: Apache Camel 4.22.0 adds camel-mcp-server, letting developers turn Camel routes into MCP tools discoverable and callable by any MCP-compatible client, plus a camel-ai-tool discoverable by every AI framework.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Enterprise integration middleware exposing routes as MCP tools means decades of existing EAI connectors become instantly agent-callable — a fast, cheap path to agentic enterprise integration.
insights.quote: the camel-mcp-server that allows developers to create Camel routes to become an MCP tool that any MCP-compatible client can discover and call

insights.claim: A2A Java SDK 1.2.0, which implements the Agent2Agent Protocol for running agentic applications as A2AServers, adds a TaskStreamLifecycleHook interface for observing task stream lifecycle events and on-demand closure of ChildQueue instances via StreamCloseHandle.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Lifecycle hooks and forced stream closure are operability primitives — a sign A2A implementations are moving from demo to production concerns.
insights.locator: The release of A2A Java SDK 1.2.0

insights.claim: A2A Java SDK 1.2.0 adds the ability for non-CDI integrations to reuse existing authorization flows, removing a dependency-injection framework constraint on agent server deployments.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Decoupling from CDI widens the deployable surface for A2A servers into non-Jakarta Java stacks.
insights.locator: The release of A2A Java SDK 1.2.0

insights.claim: Gradle 9.7.0 elevates the Isolated Projects performance feature from experimental to incubating, moving Gradle's parallel configuration work one step closer to general availability.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Isolated Projects is Gradle's main lever on large-monorepo build times — the promotion is the signal to start piloting it.
insights.locator: The release of Gradle 9.7.0 delivers notable changes

insights.claim: Gradle 9.7.0 also improves the Configuration Cache by caching the result of the configuration phase and reusing it for subsequent builds, and makes trusted PGP keys easier to document and signing-key rotations easier to discover.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Supply-chain ergonomics (key rotation discoverability) appearing alongside performance work shows build tools absorbing dependency-integrity responsibilities.
insights.locator: The release of Gradle 9.7.0 delivers notable changes

insights.claim: The article's body covers a fifth milestone release of Apache Grails 8.0.0 — including a GlobalGrailsClassInjectorTransformation refactor with isolated-build behavior — even though the headline and opening paragraph both name Groovy 8.0 as the milestone release.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: A naming discrepancy between headline and body; readers tracking Groovy releases from the headline alone would be misinformed.
insights.locator: The fifth milestone release of Apache Grails 8.0.0

insights.claim: Both JDK 27 (Build 34) and JDK 28 (Build 10) early-access builds shipped in the same week, confirming OpenJDK is running two release trains concurrently in the run-up to JDK 27's RC.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Overlapping trains means JDK 28 features like JEP 535 and value objects are already accumulating while 27 is still stabilizing — plan upgrade testing for both.
insights.locator: Build 10 of the JDK 28 early-access builds
